subject: English
description: Question tags — short interrogative add-ons; auxiliary verb agreement, polarity flip, common rules and exceptions.

questions.stem: Choose the correct question tag: 'She is a doctor, ___?'
questions.explanation: RULE 1 — POLARITY FLIP: positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. 'She IS a doctor' (positive) → tag must be NEGATIVE: 'isn't she'. RULE 2 — SAME AUXILIARY: use the SAME helping verb as in the main clause. Here 'is' → 'isn't'. RULE 3 — PRONOUN AGREEMENT: subject must match — 'she' → 'she'. STRUCTURE: [aux + n't + pronoun]. EXAMPLES: 'You are coming, AREN'T YOU?' 'He has finished, HASN'T HE?' 'They will arrive, WON'T THEY?' 'She doesn't know, DOES SHE?' EXCEPTIONS: (a) 'I am' → 'AREN'T I?' (idiomatic, never 'amn't I'). (b) 'Let's go' → 'SHALL WE?' (c) 'Open the door' (imperative) → 'WILL YOU?' or 'WON'T YOU?' (d) 'Nobody knows' (negative meaning even if no 'not') → 'DO THEY?' PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CHSL, IBPS Clerk regularly test 1-2 question-tag Qs per paper.

questions.stem: Pick the correct tag: 'Let's go for a walk, ___?'
questions.explanation: SPECIAL RULE: 'Let's' (= let us, suggestion) is followed by 'SHALL WE?' as a tag. EXAMPLES: 'Let's eat, shall we?' 'Let's not argue, shall we?' Even if 'Let's' is preceded by 'not' (negative suggestion), the tag stays 'shall we'. NOT TO BE CONFUSED: 'Let me know' is NOT 'let's' — it's 'let' (verb of permission), so tag = 'will you?' RULE FOR IMPERATIVES: 'Open the door' → 'WILL YOU?' (polite request) or 'WON'T YOU?' / 'CAN YOU?' / 'COULD YOU?' depending on tone. NEGATIVE IMPERATIVE: 'Don't smoke here' → 'WILL YOU?' (still 'will you', not flipped!). FORMAL vs INFORMAL: 'shall we' is fairly formal — used in invitations, polite suggestions. INFORMAL alternative: 'okay?' or 'right?' (not standard for exam English). PYQ ANGLE: 'Let's...shall we' is a top-3 question-tag exception, tested in CGL & IBPS.

options.option_text: am not I alone alone alone

questions.explanation: FAMOUS EXCEPTION: 'I am' takes 'AREN'T I?' as a tag — even though grammatically you'd expect 'amn't I'. Reason: 'amn't' is awkward to pronounce; 'aren't I' is the accepted idiomatic alternative. EXAMPLES: 'I am right, aren't I?' 'I'm late, aren't I?' NOTE: 'aren't' is normally a contraction of 'are not' — but in this single context, it's a fixed idiom meaning 'am I not?' DIALECT VARIATIONS: Scottish/Irish English sometimes uses 'amn't I' colloquially. American formal: 'am I not?' (very stilted). INVERTED INTERROGATIVE: 'AM I NOT a teacher?' is the formal/literary alternative — full version. POSITIVE TAG: 'I am NOT a teacher, AM I?' (positive tag for negative statement). PYQ ANGLE: 'aren't I' is a SSC, RRB, IBPS Clerk top-10 grammar exception — appears 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests EXCEPTIONS to standard rules — high-IQ grammar discipline.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tag: 'Nobody complained about the food, ___?'
questions.explanation: TRICKY RULE: 'Nobody', 'no one', 'none', 'nothing' carry NEGATIVE meaning — even though no 'not' appears, the sentence is treated as NEGATIVE → tag becomes POSITIVE. So 'Nobody complained' (negative meaning) → 'DID THEY?' (positive tag). PRONOUN AGREEMENT: 'nobody/no one' takes 'they/them' in tags (and elsewhere) — singular but referenced as plural for inclusivity. EXAMPLES: 'Nothing went wrong, did it?' 'No one called you, did they?' 'Nobody objects, do they?' WORDS WITH IMPLIED NEGATIVE: 'hardly', 'rarely', 'scarcely', 'barely', 'seldom' also flip the tag to positive. 'He hardly ever smiles, DOES HE?' 'She rarely visits, DOES SHE?' EXAMINER MINDSET: tests SEMANTIC negation — beyond surface-level 'not'-spotting. PYQ ANGLE: SSC, IBPS test 'nobody/hardly/rarely + do they' pattern 1-2× per paper.

options.option_text: do you — flip negative to positive
are you alone alone alone (option here)

questions.explanation: POLARITY FLIP: 'You don't smoke' is NEGATIVE (contains 'don't') → tag must be POSITIVE: 'do you?' AUXILIARY: 'don't' is the helping verb here (do + n't), so tag uses 'do' (positive form). AGREEMENT: 'you' → 'you' (same pronoun). FULL EXAMPLES: 'They aren't coming, ARE THEY?' 'He didn't reply, DID HE?' 'It hasn't rained, HAS IT?' 'She won't agree, WILL SHE?' PRACTICE — flip polarity of the auxiliary while keeping pronoun: aren't → are; doesn't → does; haven't → have; won't → will; can't → can; shouldn't → should. PYQ ANGLE: this is the most-tested basic question-tag pattern in SSC CHSL Tier 1 — 1-2 Qs guaranteed per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing simple polarity-flip discipline. EXAM TIP: identify the AUXILIARY first, then flip polarity.

questions.stem: Choose the correct tag: 'Open the window, ___?'
questions.explanation: IMPERATIVE TAG RULE: For commands/requests, the standard tag is 'WILL YOU?' or its variants 'WON'T YOU?', 'CAN YOU?', 'COULD YOU?'. 'Will you' is most common and neutral. EXAMPLES: 'Pass the salt, will you?' 'Help me, won't you?' 'Wait here, can you?' 'Don't smoke, will you?' (Negative imperative still uses 'will you' — NO polarity flip for imperatives.) NUANCE: 'Won't you?' is more polite/inviting; 'Will you?' is more direct; 'Could you?' is the most formal/polite. NEGATIVE IMPERATIVES: 'Don't be late, will you?' / 'Don't go out, will you?' — exception to polarity flip rule because imperatives are not pronouncements (no auxiliary verb in main clause). 'LET'S' is a SUGGESTION, not a true imperative → uses 'shall we'. PYQ ANGLE: imperative-tag is a 1-mark Q in SSC CHSL, IBPS Clerk. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing the imperative-special-case rule.

questions.stem: Pick the correct tag: 'There is little water in the bottle, ___?'
questions.explanation: TWO TRICKS: (1) 'LITTLE' (without 'a') means 'almost none' — NEGATIVE meaning. So tag flips to POSITIVE → 'is there?' (NOT 'isn't there'). (2) 'There is/are' constructions use 'there' as the dummy subject in the tag — NOT 'it'. So 'there' is correct. KEY DISTINCTIONS: 'a little' = some/positive; 'little' = almost none/negative. 'a few' = some/positive; 'few' = almost none/negative. 'There is A LITTLE water, isn't there?' (positive). 'There is LITTLE water, IS there?' (negative-meaning, flip to positive). EXAMPLES: 'Few people came, did they?' 'A few people came, didn't they?' THERE-CONSTRUCTION TAGS: 'There is a problem, isn't there?' / 'There were no flights, were there?' (already negative → positive tag, with 'were'). PYQ ANGLE: 'little/few + tag' is a top-5 grammar pitfall — appears in SSC, banking 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests subtle SEMANTIC distinctions (positive vs negative meaning).

questions.stem: He will be joining us for the annual conference tomorrow, ___?

options.option_text: will he (positive tag, wrong polarity here)

questions.explanation: With a positive auxiliary 'will', the question tag must be its contracted negative form 'won't he'. 'Isn't he' is the most common error — it incorrectly picks the 'be' verb from 'will be' instead of using the modal 'will'. 'Wouldn't he' shifts the mood to conditional, changing meaning entirely.

questions.stem: They have been waiting for the results for over an hour, ___?

options.option_text: did they (past simple tag, wrong tense)
hadn't they (past perfect tag, wrong tense)

questions.explanation: The main clause uses present perfect 'have been', so the tag auxiliary must also be present perfect 'haven't they'. 'Have they' is wrong polarity (positive after a positive clause). 'Did they' reverts to past simple. 'Hadn't they' incorrectly shifts to past perfect tense.

questions.stem: She used to work as a government nurse before her marriage, ___?

options.option_text: didn't she (standard negative tag for 'used to')
hadn't she (past perfect tag, wrong auxiliary)

questions.explanation: In standard modern exam usage, 'used to' forms its question tag with the auxiliary 'did', giving 'didn't she'. 'Usedn't she' is an archaic British form not accepted in competitive exams. 'Wasn't she' is the most common error — it treats 'used' as a form of 'be', which is incorrect.

questions.stem: You had better consult a specialist before undergoing the surgery, ___?

options.option_text: hadn't you (correct negative tag for 'had better')

questions.explanation: 'Had better' is a semi-fixed modal expression; its question tag must use 'hadn't + subject'. 'Should you not' is wrong because 'had better' is not paraphrasable as 'should' for tagging. 'Wouldn't you' is the most tempting distractor — test-takers confuse 'would' with 'had' in this expression.

questions.stem: Everyone in the department has submitted the progress report, ___?

options.option_text: have they (plural auxiliary, wrong verb form)
hasn't he (singular pronoun, wrong gender used)
haven't they (negative tag, plural pronoun correct)

questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is grammatically singular (hence 'has') but is referred to by 'they' in modern standard English for the pronoun in the tag. The auxiliary echoes 'has' as its negative 'haven't'. 'Have they' wrongly keeps the auxiliary plural. 'Hasn't he' assumes a masculine pronoun, which is no longer standard.

questions.stem: Neither the principal nor the teachers were consulted about the new policy, ___?

options.option_text: were they (positive tag, correct polarity here)
weren't they (negative tag, wrong polarity used)

questions.explanation: 'Neither...nor' is inherently negative in meaning, so the question tag must be positive — giving 'were they'. By the proximity rule, the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'teachers' (plural) → 'were'. 'Wasn't he' is the most tempting error: test-takers match the tag to only 'principal' (singular), ignoring proximity and polarity rules simultaneously.

questions.stem: Seldom does he visit his ageing parents these days, ___?

options.option_text: doesn't he (negative tag, creates double negative)
does he (positive tag matching 'seldom' as negative adverb)
did he (past simple tag, wrong tense for present sense)
isn't he (uses 'be' instead of 'do', wrong auxiliary)

questions.explanation: 'Seldom' is a negative adverb that gives the sentence a negative meaning, triggering subject-auxiliary inversion ('does he' at the front). Because the clause is already semantically negative, the tag must be positive: 'does he'. 'Doesn't he' is the classic trap — it adds a second negative, making a double-negative construction. 'Did he' wrongly switches to past tense.
